I have been a guide in Ljubljana for twenty-two years, and the travelers have changed more than the city. People used to arrive in big groups, with a very structured day: the castle at nine, the bridges at eleven, lunch at one. They used to follow my umbrella and take a photograph of everything. Today I see many more solo travelers, and a lot of them are over sixty. They don't want ten places. They want two, at their own pace. They ask me where I buy my coffee, not where the famous view is. I still give a guided tour, but now it is the first morning, not the whole trip. After that, they try to blend in. And honestly, the ones who stay a full week usually do.

When I was young, I didn't use to plan anything, and I was proud of it. I used to arrive in a city with no hotel and no map. Then I got older, and I became the opposite. Every trip was structured, and every museum was booked a month before. Last year my daughter said one sentence that changed my mind. She said: Dad, you used to be fun. So on my last trip to Slovenia, I left two days completely empty. On one of them I took a bus to a small lake, ate fish with a family I didn't know, and missed the last bus home. It was the best day of the trip. My preference now is somewhere in the middle: a plan for the mornings, and nothing for the afternoons.

First he spent thirty years on work trips, with a hotel near the office and dinner at the same restaurant every night. Then he retired and booked one week in Lisbon, his first trip as a solo traveler. After that he got lost in Alfama on the second day, and a woman at a bakery explained the street to him with her hands. At that point he understood that the spontaneous afternoon was the only one he could still describe hour by hour. In the end he changed his preference: fewer cities, more days, and a slow pace in a normal neighborhood.
